lede: Four words change the whole question: given that. They tell you something has already happened, so the group you are choosing from is smaller than it was. Everything about conditional probability is deciding which smaller group goes on the bottom of the fraction.
can: Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree
Use the formula on the sheet, with the condition on the denominator
Spot when one event sits inside another, so the numerator is the smaller one

md:
A cafe asks 250 customers whether they drink tea or coffee and which age group they are in.
Ask 'what is the probability a customer drinks tea' and the group is all 250. Add 'given that the customer is under 30' and the group is only the under-30s. Nothing else about the table has changed.

md: Think of the condition as a cover laid over the table. Everything outside the named group is hidden, and the question is now about the people still showing. The count on top must come from inside that group, and the total underneath is the size of the group itself.

stem: Find the tea row's total and the 30-and-over column's total on the cafe table.

steps.decision: A row's cells add to its total.
A column works the same way.
The row totals add to everybody asked, and so do the column totals.

prompt: On the cafe table, how many of the 250 customers are under 30?
explain: As in step 2 of See it, add the column's cells: $42 + 108 = 150$. That total is the group any 'given under 30' question divides by.

twin.explain: The column's cells add to its total: $19 + 28 = 47$.

md: 'The probability of tea, given under 30' is written $P(\text{tea} \mid \text{under 30})$. The upright bar is read 'given'. The condition is the group you are now choosing from, so its total goes on the bottom.

The top of the fraction is the cell where the event meets the condition: the people in the group who also do the thing asked about. So the top always sits inside the bottom, and a conditional probability is never more than 1. An answer above 1 means the fraction is upside down.

steps.working: The group: the 100 customers aged 30 and over
steps.decision: The condition names the whole.
The cell where coffee meets the condition's column.
The cell over the condition's total.

prompt: On the cafe table, which total is the denominator of $P(\text{tea} \mid \text{under 30})$?
explain: As in step 1 of See it, the condition names the group: here the under-30s, so those 150 are the group you are choosing from. Dividing by 250 would ignore the condition altogether.

optionNotes.why: Tea is the event asked about, not the condition; dividing by its total answers 'under 30, given tea'.
Everybody is the whole only before the condition; 'given under 30' shrinks it to that column.

twin.prompt: In a survey of 200 pupils, 90 walk to school. Which total is the denominator of $P(\text{late} \mid \text{walks})$?
twin.explain: The condition, walks, names the group: the 90 walkers are the whole you divide by.

optionNotes.why: Late is the event asked about; its total would answer 'walks, given late'.
The 200 is the whole only before the condition; 'given walks' shrinks it to the 90.

md: The formula printed on page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, is the table's share written in probabilities. A table question can be answered straight from the counts; a tree question, where only probabilities are given, uses the formula as printed.

Read the formula from the bar outwards. Whatever follows the bar is the condition, and its probability goes underneath; the top is the chance that both happen at once. Writing the two pieces in words first, 'both' over 'the condition', keeps the fraction the right way up before any number goes in.

stem: Show that $\dfrac{42}{150}$, the share of the under-30s who drink tea, is $\dfrac{P(\text{tea and under 30})}{P(\text{under 30})}$.

steps.decision: Divide the top and the bottom by the 250 asked: the fraction does not change.
The top has become a probability of both at once.
The bottom has become the condition's probability.
With $A$ for tea and $B$ for under 30: the sheet's formula.

prompt: In $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, which probability goes on the bottom?
explain: As step 3 of See it shows, the bottom came from the condition's total, so it is the condition's probability. The numerator is the probability that both happen.

optionNotes.why: $A$ is the event asked about; dividing by its probability answers '$B$ given $A$'.
Both together is the top of the fraction; the bottom is the group the condition names.

twin.prompt: In $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, which probability goes on the top?
twin.explain: The top is the share of the condition's group where $A$ happens as well: both at once, $P(A \cap B)$.

optionNotes.why: $A$ on its own counts cases outside the condition too; only those in both belong on top.
$P(B)$ is the condition's probability, the bottom of the fraction.

text: Why a share can come out bigger

title: Why dividing works
md: Conditioning is rescaling. The condition's probability is the new whole, so dividing by it turns the joint probability into a share of the smaller group. That is also why a conditional probability can be larger than the joint one it came from.

That gives a quick check on any answer. A conditional probability is at least as big as the joint probability it came from, and at most 1. If a 'given' answer comes out smaller than the joint probability, something has been multiplied that should have been divided.

stem: Rescale the cafe's $P(\text{tea and under 30})$ by $P(\text{under 30})$.

steps.decision: The joint probability, a share of the whole survey.
The condition's probability: the new whole.
Bigger than the joint probability, because the group is smaller than the whole survey.

explain: As in step 3 of See it, rescale by the condition: $0.21 \div 0.28 = 0.75$. The share of the smaller group is larger than the joint probability, as it always is when $P(B)$ is below 1.

steps.decision: The condition is the under-30 column: its total underneath.
The condition is the coffee row now: the same cell on top, a different total underneath.

prompt: On the cafe table, 42 of the 75 tea drinkers are under 30. What is $P(\text{under 30} \mid \text{tea})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: As in step 2 of See it, the condition is the row this time: $\dfrac{42}{75}$ is $\dfrac{14}{25}$, with the tea total, 75, underneath.

twin.prompt: In a survey, 18 of the 48 cyclists are under 16. What is $P(\text{under 16} \mid \text{cycles})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
twin.explain: The condition is cycling, so the 48 cyclists are the whole: $\dfrac{18}{48} = \dfrac{3}{8}$.

text: 4. See it done: a Venn diagram

md: A Venn diagram is a two-way table drawn as circles. Each region is a cell, and a circle's total is every region inside it, the overlap included. 'Given French' makes the French circle the whole: both of its regions go underneath, and the overlap, the students who take both, goes on top.

text: 5. From a tree: add the branches

md: A match is cancelled more often after rain. $P(\text{rain}) = 0.3$; the match is cancelled with probability $0.5$ after rain and $0.1$ on a dry day. There are no counts, so each path is a product.

On a tree the condition is usually an outcome at the end of the branches, such as 'cancelled', and more than one path can reach it. Its probability is every one of those paths, each multiplied along and then added. Leaving a path out makes the denominator too small and the answer too big.

stem: On the match tree, find the two branches that end in 'cancelled'.

steps.decision: Multiply along the branch.
The other path to the same outcome.

prompt: On the match tree, the rain-and-cancelled branch is $0.15$ and the dry-and-cancelled branch is $0.07$. What is $P(\text{cancelled})$?
explain: The two branches in See it both end in 'cancelled' and cannot both happen, so they add: $0.15 + 0.07 = 0.22$.

twin.prompt: Two branches of a tree end in 'late': $0.12$ and $0.15$. What is $P(\text{late})$?
twin.explain: Separate branches to the same outcome add: $0.12 + 0.15 = 0.27$.

md: The numerator is one branch; the denominator is every branch that satisfies the condition. Finding one of the two and stopping is the commonest way this part is lost.

title: What the reports keep finding
md: Candidates often reach the right numerator, or the right denominator, but never combine the two. Write the formula with the condition named before any number goes in.

stem: Given that the match was cancelled, find the probability that the day was dry.

steps.decision: The numerator: the one branch that is dry and cancelled.
The denominator: every branch that ends in 'cancelled'.
Combine the two pieces: about 0.32.

title: Conditional Probability
why: Conditional probability from tables and from trees, in the notation this unit uses. The reversed-condition trap and the nested-event case are the steps this unit adds on top.

prompt: Using the match tree, $P(\text{rain and cancelled}) = 0.15$ and $P(\text{cancelled}) = 0.22$. What is $P(\text{rain} \mid \text{cancelled})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: As in step 3 of See it: $\dfrac{0.15}{0.22}$ is $\dfrac{15}{22}$, which is 0.682. Giving 0.15 on its own leaves the division undone.

twin.prompt: $P(\text{late and wet}) = 0.07$ and $P(\text{late}) = 0.08$. What is $P(\text{wet} \mid \text{late})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
twin.explain: One branch over the condition's total: $0.07 \div 0.08 = 0.875$.

text: 7. When one event sits inside the other

md: When one event lies wholly inside the other, the two together are just the smaller one: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)$. There is nothing to multiply on the numerator.

To spot it, ask whether one event forces the other. If every outcome of $A$ is also an outcome of $B$, then $A$ sits inside $B$, and 'both' adds nothing to $A$. Exam questions hide this in wording such as 'exactly three' inside 'at least two', or 'all the same' inside 'at least two the same'.

stem: Four coins are tossed. Find $P(\text{four heads} \mid \text{at least two heads})$.

steps.working: Four heads is at least two heads, so $P(A \cap B) = P(\text{four heads})$
steps.decision: The inner event on its own is the top.
Four heads in one way of 16; at least two heads in 11 ways.
Divide; the sixteenths cancel.

prompt: Every first-team player at a school plays football, so 'first team' lies entirely inside 'plays football'. What is $P(\text{first team and plays football})$?
explain: As with the coins in See it, the inner event decides: every first-team player already plays football, so the two together are the first team on its own. Multiplying would treat them as unrelated.

optionNotes.why: Multiplying treats the events as independent, but being in the first team settles 'plays football' completely.
Football players include those outside the first team, who are not in both.

twin.prompt: 'Exactly three sixes' lies entirely inside 'at least one six'. What is $P(\text{exactly three sixes and at least one six})$?
options: $P(\text{exactly three sixes}) \times P(\text{at least one six})$
twin.explain: Exactly three sixes is already at least one six, so 'both' is the inner event alone.

optionNotes.option: $P(\text{exactly three sixes}) \times P(\text{at least one six})$
optionNotes.why: A product needs independent events; three sixes settles 'at least one' completely.
The larger event includes one or two sixes, which are not exactly three.

text: 8. Expected numbers from a conditional probability

md: A conditional probability scales a group, and the group it scales is the one named in the condition.

An expected number is the size of a group multiplied by a probability. With a condition, check that the group in the question is the group the condition names, then multiply its size by the conditional probability. The result is an estimate of how many, so it need not be a whole number.

stem: The cafe expects 500 customers under 30 next week. How many would you expect to drink tea?

steps.decision: Scale the group the condition names by the conditional probability.
The whole survey's share would give far too few: next week's customers are all under 30.

prompt: In the cafe survey, 108 of the 150 customers under 30 drink coffee. The cafe expects 500 customers under 30 next week. How many of them would you expect to drink coffee?
explain: As in step 1 of See it: $500 \times \dfrac{108}{150} = 360$. The 500 is the group the condition names, and with the 140 tea drinkers it makes the 500.

twin.prompt: A shop expects 50 customers under 16 next week, and $P(\text{juice} \mid \text{under 16}) = 0.3$. How many would you expect to buy juice?
twin.explain: Scale the group the condition names: $50 \times 0.3 = 15$.

text: Exam twists: where the condition hides

md: **No 'given' in the words.** Summer 2023 stated the condition as a sentence of its own, and many answers came over the whole group. 'A customer picked from those aged 30 and over' is a condition too.
**The condition is the second stage.** Summer 2025 gave the result of a second set and asked about the first. The bottom is every branch whose second stage meets the condition.

stem: Two beads come from 6 red and 4 green, without replacement. Given that the second is red, find the probability that the first was red.

steps.working: Out of 90: red then red 30, green then red 24
steps.decision: Every ordered pair counted out of the same total; both of these end in a red second bead.
The branch with a red first over every branch with a red second.

prompt: Two beads are taken without replacement from 6 red and 4 green. Given that the second bead is green, what is the probability that the first was red? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: As in See it, count out of 90: red then green is 24 and green then green is 12. Given a green second bead: $\dfrac{24}{24 + 12}$, which is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

twin.prompt: Two beads are taken without replacement from 5 red and 3 green. Given that the second is green, what is the probability that the first was red? Give a fraction or a decimal.
twin.explain: Red then green is 5 × 3 = 15 ways, green then green 3 × 2 = 6: $\dfrac{15}{21} = \dfrac{5}{7}$.

text: Exam twists: a 'not' and a missing overlap

md: **The condition is a 'not'.** Summer 2025 also conditioned on a student who does not study a subject. Given the match was not cancelled, the whole is $P(\text{played}) = 1 - 0.22 = 0.78$, the two 'played' branches together.
**The overlap is not given.** When only $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cup B)$ are known, the addition rule finds the overlap first.

steps.decision: The addition rule, used backwards, gives the overlap.
Then the overlap over the condition's probability.

explain: As in See it, the overlap first: $0.6 + 0.45 - 0.75 = 0.3$. The condition is $A$ this time, so $0.3 \div 0.6 = 0.5$.

text: Going further: 'at least one' as the condition

md: The hardest shape on the paper: Summer 2026 ended its tree question with a condition of 'during the weekend', that is, on at least one day. Snow falls on each day of a weekend with probability $0.1$, the days independent.

stem: Given that it snows on at least one day of the weekend, find the probability that it does not snow on Sunday.

steps.decision: The whole: everything except no snow on either day.
Given snow on at least one day, no snow on Sunday means snow on Saturday only.
The top sits inside the condition, so nothing more is multiplied.

prompt: On the same snowy weekend, given that it snows on at least one of the two days, what is the probability that it snows on both? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: As in step 3 of See it, the top sits inside the condition: both days is $0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01$, so $0.01 \div 0.19 = \dfrac{1}{19}$.

twin.prompt: Rain falls on each day of a weekend with probability 0.9, the days independent. Given rain on at least one day, what is the probability of rain on both? Give a fraction or a decimal.
twin.explain: Both is $0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.81$ and at least one is $0.99$, so $0.81 \div 0.99 = \dfrac{9}{11}$.

md:
Read the condition first and write down the group it names.
Use $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, with the condition underneath.
Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree, in either direction.
Use the inner event as the numerator when one event sits inside another.
Scale the group the condition names when an expected number is asked for.

This is the last part of a probability question, and the one that separates the strongest. It is worded 'given that', or 'a person is chosen from those who', for two or three marks. The first mark is the right denominator; the last is the divided answer. Stuck: write the formula with the condition named, then fill in the two pieces.
